data.text/markdown:
Trajectory families and TP-Space (PTGs)

This notebook uses the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3) to explore Parameterized Trajectory Generators (PTGs), the core of MRPT's reactive navigator. A PTG is a family of kinematically feasible paths that start at the robot, indexed by one parameter ||(\alpha \in (-\pi, \pi]||). Any point ||((x, y)||) reached by those paths gets new coordinates ||((\alpha, d)||): which path reaches it, and after how many meters. In this TP-Space (Trajectory Parameter Space) every path becomes a straight radial line, so a differential-drive robot can be treated as a point that moves freely in any direction, and obstacle avoidance becomes much simpler. It uses the mrpt.nav module: CParameterizedTrajectoryGenerator (its factory CreatePTG(), initialize() and the Workspace to TP-Space map inverseMap_WS2TP()), with the PTG classes CPTG_DiffDrive_C, CPTG_DiffDrive_alpha, CPTG_DiffDrive_CS and CPTG_Holo_Blend. Move the sliders: change the PTG family, the robot speed limits, the number of paths, or drag the wall around and watch how it maps into TP-Space.

data.text/html: PTG parameters

data.text/markdown:
1. Create the PTG

PTGs are created by class name with a factory, from parameters in MRPT INI config-file format. The key ones are the robot speed limits, the number of discrete paths (the resolution in ||(\alpha||)) and the reference distance: paths are only simulated up to that length, which is then used to normalize TP-Space distances to ||([0, 1]||). initialize() simulates the paths and builds look-up tables (cached on disk, so it only takes a while the first time for each set of parameters).

data.text/html:
[PTG]
refDistance = 3.0
num_paths = 31
v_max_mps = 1.0
w_max_dps = 60
K = 1
resolution = 0.25     # cell size of the collision look-up table (m)
cte_a0v_deg = 57      # only for alpha-A
cte_a0w_deg = 57      # only for alpha-A
T_ramp_max = 0.8      # only for holonomic
robot_radius = 0.35   # only for holonomic
shape_x0 = -0.2
shape_y0 = 0.3
shape_x1 = 0.5
shape_y1 = 0.3
shape_x2 = 0.5
shape_y2 = -0.3
shape_x3 = -0.2
shape_y3 = -0.3
ptg.getDescription(): CPTG_DiffDrive_alpha,av=57deg,aw=57deg,K=1 ptg.isInitialized(): True ptg.getPathCount(): 31 paths

data.text/markdown:
2. From Workspace to TP-Space

inverseMap_WS2TP(x, y) answers the key question of TP-Space navigation: which path ||(k||) (that is, which ||(\alpha||)) passes through the point ||((x, y)||), and at which normalized distance ||(d||) along it? We call it for every point of a grid around the robot. Then, the curves of constant ||(k||) are the trajectories of the family (left plot, drawn where ||(k||) changes from one path to the next), and the curves of constant ||(d||) are the points the robot reaches after traveling the same distance. In TP-Space (right plot) the same paths are just straight rays. Colors encode ||(\alpha||): blue paths turn right, gray ones go straight ahead, and red ones turn left. The wall below is an obstacle. Each of its points is also mapped to TP-Space, and every path is cut at the first obstacle it meets: this free distance per direction is what MRPT feeds to a holonomic obstacle avoidance method (e.g. ND or VFF) to pick the best ||(\alpha||). For simplicity the robot is treated as a point here (MRPT's navigator also accounts for its footprint).

data.text/html: Obstacle

data.text/markdown: The wall blocks 10 of 31 paths. The closest obstacle along a path is at 1.37 m (path k = 12, α = -35°).

Things to try:
  • C paths are circular arcs with radius proportional to ||(1/\alpha||); the tightest turn radius is ||(v_{max} / \omega_{max}||), so points inside the two tightest circles cannot be reached.
  • α-A paths turn quickly towards heading ||(\alpha||) and then go straight, so they cover the space around and behind the robot.
  • Reduce the number of paths to see the coarser TP-Space discretization: a narrow wall may then fall between two paths.
  • Enable Drive backwards to get the mirrored family used for reversing (differential-drive PTGs only).

Run it on your computer (Linux, Python 3.11 to 3.14): 
uvx marimo edit --sandbox https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MRPT/mrpt-notebooks/main/notebooks/ptg_trajectories.py
More MRPT Python examples: mrpt_examples_py.
